Orchot Tzadikim 1:2: The first gate: we shall speak in it of the trait of pride. And it is well that it happens to come first among all the gates, because of man's duty to keep himself apart from it, for it is an opening to many evils, and we have not seen any trait as harmful as this one. Therefore a person must use wisdom to guide it into its proper conduct, and to push it away in a place where it is not fitting.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:3: Pride is the coin that the Holy One, blessed be He, rejected, and He warned us of it in His Torah, as it is said (Deuteronomy 6:12), "Take heed lest you forget the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt." For the proud man forgets his Maker, as it is written (Deuteronomy 8:13-18), "and your herds and your flocks multiply, and your silver and gold multiply for you... and your heart grows haughty and you forget the Lord your God... and you say in your heart, my own strength and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth. But you shall remember the Lord your God, for it is He who gives you strength to get wealth." And of the king it is said (Deuteronomy 17:20), "that his heart not be lifted up above his brothers." If the Torah warned even the king, how much more so ordinary men, that they not lord it one over another.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:4: Pride divides into two parts: one is a person's pride in his body, and the second part is a person's pride in the virtues of wisdom and in his deeds.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:5: A person's pride in his body has two parts: one good, and one bad. And this is the bad pride of a person in his body: when pride grows powerful in a person's heart, it then rules over the person from the crown of his head to the sole of his foot — in his head and his throat, as it is written (Isaiah 3:16), "Because the daughters of Zion are haughty and walk with necks outstretched"; in his hands and his feet, as it is written (Psalms 36:12), "Let not the foot of pride come against me, and let not the hand of the wicked drive me away."
Orchot Tzadikim 1:6: And for the sin of the "foot of pride" the daughter of Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon was punished, decreed to sit in a brothel. For once she walked before the great men of Rome, and heard them say, "How lovely are the steps of this young woman!" — and from then on she made her steps more precise (Avodah Zarah 18a).
Orchot Tzadikim 1:7: In the eyes, as it is written (Proverbs 6:17), "haughty eyes."
Orchot Tzadikim 1:8: In the ears: he will not listen to the words of the wretched poor. In the flaring of his nostrils: when he stands near the poor or enters their homes, they seem repulsive in his eyes. And even in his words he speaks arrogantly, insolently, against the righteous.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:9: It is also recognizable in matters of food and drink, and in wearing garments of pride, the garments of the gentile. And of this we were warned in the Torah of Moses, as it is said (Leviticus 20:23), "and you shall not walk in the statutes of the nation," and it is written (Leviticus 18:3), "and you shall not walk in their statutes," and it is said (Deuteronomy 12:30), "take heed lest you be ensnared following them" — all of this warns of one and the same matter, that Israel be set apart in its clothing, in its speech, and in all its customs from the gentiles. And so it says (Leviticus 20:26), "and I have set you apart from the peoples."
Orchot Tzadikim 1:10: The proud are held in abomination in the eyes of the Lord, as it is said (Proverbs 16:5), "An abomination to the Lord is every haughty heart." And he is handed over to his own inclination, for the Lord's help is not with him, since he is an abomination to the Lord. And even if he has not shown pride toward any person, neither in speech nor in deed, but is proud only in his heart — he is called "an abomination," as it is said, "An abomination to the Lord is every haughty heart" — even if his haughtiness is only in his heart, he is called "an abomination."
Orchot Tzadikim 1:11: Our Sages said: whoever has coarseness of spirit is as though he worshipped idols; here it is written (Proverbs 16:5), "An abomination to the Lord is every haughty heart," and there it is written (Deuteronomy 7:26), "You shall not bring an abomination into your house." And some say: it is as though he committed sexual immorality, as it is written (Leviticus 18:27), "for all these abominations have the men of the land done." And some say: it is as though he built a high place [for idolatry] (Sotah 4b). And they said: any person who has coarseness of spirit is diminished, as it is said (Job 24:24), "They are exalted a little while, and then are gone." And he deserves to be cut down like an asherah-tree, as it is said (Isaiah 10:33), "and the lofty of stature shall be cut down." And his dust is never stirred up again, and the Divine Presence wails over him. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: I and he cannot dwell together in the world, as it is said (Psalms 101:5), "Him that has a haughty eye and a proud heart I cannot endure" (Sotah 5a).
Orchot Tzadikim 1:12: And they said: this one who is haughty is not even tolerated by the members of his own household, as it is said (Habakkuk 2:5), "a haughty man shall not abide" — not even in his own dwelling (Bava Batra 98a).
Orchot Tzadikim 1:13: Pride leads to the pursuit of wealth, in order to rule over people. You already know what happened to Korach and his congregation because of his pride, for he sought greatness and took an eminence that had not been given to him from Heaven. And through this he entered into strife, and from the strife came envy and hatred. And all these are very base traits, as will be explained, with God's help.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:14: In sum: whoever adorns his body in order to feel pride has thereby forgotten the Blessed Lord, and will not concern himself with the commandments, nor pursue good deeds — for all his intent is upon himself, to adorn his perishing body, whose end is worms. And one who adorns his body is close to lewdness, for he will show himself before women to find favor in their eyes, and through this he will draw near to them, and come to levity and lightheadedness.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:15: And also the woman who adorns herself before men — by this she kindles their hearts and brings improper thoughts into their hearts; and for this her punishment is very great, for she places a stumbling-block before many. Behold, the Sages forbade gazing even at the colored garments of women spread out on a wall to dry, even when she is not wearing them (Avodah Zarah 20b) — how much more so is there great punishment for a woman who adorns herself before men who gaze at her.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:16: And further, pride leads to desire, for one who is proud has a broad heart that craves everything. And desire is the worst trait of all traits, for out of his pride he will crave to clothe himself in costly garments, to build great palaces, and to eat fine foods — for the proud man always covets lofty things, and perhaps he cannot afford them, and through this he comes to theft and robbery. For the heart of the proud man is covetous, and as broad as the sea in seeking to grow rich, and he will never be content with his own portion, for whatever he has will seem small in his eyes, in view of the great expenses of his craving for pride. And further, pride causes a person to be unable to bear the yoke of his fellow creatures. And there is no need to elaborate on the lowliness of one who cannot bear with others, for it is known to all.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:17: And this is the good pride of the body: perhaps a person will say, since pride is so bad a trait, I shall keep away from it all the more — so that I will not eat meat nor drink wine, nor marry a wife, nor dwell in a pleasant home, nor wear pleasant clothing but only sackcloth and coarse wool, torn and filthy; and I will use dirty and repulsive vessels, and I will not wash my face, hands, and feet until my complexion turns dark compared to other people — all this in order to remove himself from pride, to the point where he can remove himself no further.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:18: One who follows this path is called "a sinner." Behold, it says regarding the Nazirite (Numbers 6:11), "and he shall atone for him for having sinned regarding the soul." The Sages said (Ta'anit 11a): if this one, who deprived himself of nothing but wine, is called "a sinner," how much more so one who deprives himself of everything. Our Sages said (Yerushalmi Nedarim 9:1): is it not enough for you, what the Torah has forbidden, that you must forbid yourself other things as well?! Of this matter and the like of it Solomon said (Ecclesiastes 7:16), "Do not be overly righteous, nor make yourself overly wise; why should you destroy yourself?"
Orchot Tzadikim 1:19: The straight path for a person is this: that he be clean in all his affairs, for cleanliness is a fence for good deeds. How so? He should wear middling garments, not poor garments that shame their wearer, but rather middling garments, pleasant and clean — the poor man according to his poverty and the rich man according to his wealth. And it is forbidden that a stain or a grease-spot be found on his garments, and they should not be torn, nor should they be made fancy like the garments of the coarse-spirited.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:20: His food, too, should be clean, and he should not eat royal delicacies, but rather middling food and middling drink, according to what his means afford. And he should not drink or eat from repulsive vessels, lest he transgress "do not make your souls disgusting" (Leviticus 11:43); rather, everything should be done with cleanliness.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:21: His table and his bed should also be clean, and all his affairs should be clean. His body, too, should be clean and not filthy; but he should take care to wash his face, hands, and feet, and also his whole body from time to time, as we find with Hillel the Elder (Vayikra Rabbah 34:3), that when he took leave of his disciples he would walk along with them. His disciples said to him: Rabbi, where are you going? He said to them: to perform a commandment. They said to him: and what commandment is this? He said to them: to bathe in the bathhouse. They said to him: and is this a commandment? He said to them: Yes! For if the statues of kings, which are set up in theaters and circuses, are scrubbed and polished by the one appointed over them, and he is given his food thereby, and moreover he grows great among the great men of the kingdom — I, who was created in the image and likeness [of God], as it is written (Genesis 9:6), "for in the image of God He made man" — how much more so!
Orchot Tzadikim 1:22: And further, as it is written (Proverbs 16:4), "The Lord has made everything for His own purpose" (Shabbat 50b).
Orchot Tzadikim 1:23: And whoever is careful about these matters for the sake of the commandment, and not in order to adorn himself and feel proud — even though these things appear to be pride — since his intent is for the sake of Heaven, there is in it a commandment.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:24: Pride in wisdom and good deeds has two parts: one good, one bad. The bad pride is this: he despises people in his heart and with his mouth, and everyone is small and lowly in his eyes; and he praises and glorifies himself as great in wisdom, and through this he will not admit the truth, out of the greatness of his pride. And forever his own wisdom, counsel, words, and deeds appear in his eyes to be superior to the deeds and the wise counsel of his fellows. And he constantly boasts of his wisdom and his deeds, for he desires to receive praise and honor for his upright words. And of this Solomon said (Proverbs 27:2), "Let another praise you, and not your own mouth."
Orchot Tzadikim 1:25: The proud man will always credit himself with the good. And through this he will not trouble himself over the Torah, for he is not concerned with the honor of Heaven, only that the world should acknowledge that he is a good and wise man, and with this he is satisfied. And he is always glad at the stumbling of his fellows and at their lack of knowledge, and he glorifies himself through the disgrace of his fellows. And this is one of the twenty-four things that hold back teshuvah. A person all of whose deeds are good, and who glorifies himself in them for the sake of honor, is like an important dish made with every kind of spice and the finest of perfumes, which stands too long by the fire until it scorches and turns rancid, until it is no longer fit to eat because of the bitterness of the fire's burning; so is the person who boasts of his deeds — he scorches and makes rancid his good deeds through his own praise of them. And one who boasts of wisdom and deeds that he does not have — there is no trait as bad as this one, and none to compare to it. Have not our Sages said (Yerushalmi Shevi'it 10:8): if people honor a man because they suppose he knows two tractates, when in fact he knows only one, he should tell them that he knows only one. How much more so should he not mislead the world into holding him in a great presumption that he does not deserve.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:26: And know that we are obligated that all our deeds be devoted solely to the Name of the Creator, exalted be He, both openly and in secret. And every deed of the service of God should be done to attain His will alone, without regard for the will of people, hoping for praise for one's deeds and to receive honor; rather, one should do everything for the sake of the God who looks into the heart, as the verse says (Jeremiah 17:10), "I the Lord search the heart, I try the reins," and it says (Deuteronomy 29:28), "The secret things belong to the Lord our God."
Orchot Tzadikim 1:27: Therefore, if a person is not careful, with wisdom and diligence, to save himself from pride, then even though he has Torah and good deeds in hand, he will inherit Gehinnom. For the inclination lies in wait for him, and brings arguments and proofs to bring the person to pride, so that his very wisdom will become the cause of his banishment from the world. Therefore let him not be lazy about conquering the evil inclination day after day, and this is called "the great war," as we find regarding one of the pious, who met men returning from war laden with great spoil. He said to them: you have returned from the small war, but you still have the great war ahead of you. They said to him: what is this war? He said to them: the inclination and its forces! For any enemy you have, whom you defeat once, twice, or three times, will then leave you be. But the inclination never stops attacking you, even if it has been defeated a hundred times, as our Sages said (Avot 2:4): do not trust in yourself until the day of your death — for it lies in wait for you all your days, in case you should let your guard down; and if it defeats you in the lightest of light matters, it will end by defeating you in the gravest of grave matters. And since pride is the root of many base traits, and since the inclination also joins and mixes itself into the heart of a person, and the whole business of the inclination is to deny the truth and affirm falsehood, teaching a person to become proud and bringing him proofs for it — you must therefore use wisdom against it.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:28: The first of the inclination's stratagems is that it hardens and raises up a person's heart, and sweetens for him pride and other bad traits. And even though the person knows for certain that there is transgression and iniquity in his pride, he still deliberately transgresses and becomes proud, because the inclination inflames his heart with a passion for honor, until he no longer cares about the transgression.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:29: But the person who is pure in his deeds, and does not become proud or glorify himself when he knows there is transgression in the matter — then the evil inclination will come and wage yet another war against him, to fell him and catch him in its net, and it will suggest permission and offer him reasonings that he has a commandment and a reward for that in which he glorifies and prides himself. And thus the inclination will say to him: "You have already reached the level of wisdom and piety, and it is fitting for you to seek favor and endeavor to find grace in the eyes of the world and to flatter them, revealing to them your wisdom and your righteousness so that they will love you." And it will bring you proof from the words of our Sages (Avot 3:10): whoever is pleasing to his fellow creatures is pleasing to the Omnipresent. But all this is a false proof, for that very reasoning is itself a branch of pride. Rather, the matter is as the verse says (Proverbs 16:7), "When the Lord is pleased with a man's ways, He makes even his enemies be at peace with him." And this is the explanation of the matter: if a person does not glorify himself before people, and does not endeavor to find favor in their eyes by doing his good deeds, and nonetheless they love him — this is great proof that the Holy One, blessed be He, loves him, and He has cast love for him into the hearts of people, and has set a good name for him upon their tongues. And it is true that there are people who are beloved by their fellow creatures whom the Holy One, blessed be He, hates, when they do not fulfill the commandments, for the Holy One, blessed be He, loves only those who study the Torah and fulfill it.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:30: After that the inclination will incite you to reveal your piety and your good deeds before the people, bringing the proof: "perhaps they too will do as you do." And this too stems from haughtiness: although we find that several great men praised themselves (Sukkah 28a), they did so only before their students and colleagues, so that these would follow after them and hold fast to their deeds; certainly this is a commandment, in order to make good deeds beloved to them. And even before these he should not be proud in his heart, saying "this I know" or "this I do," but before the world at large it is truly forbidden to reveal these things to them.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:31: Also, if you go about in humility, and stand to pray at length, and study regularly, the inclination will seduce you to become proud, and will say to you: "Now the people who see you will esteem and honor you for your good ways. And there is great gain in this: since you are important in their eyes, they will accept your ethical guidance and rebuke."
Orchot Tzadikim 1:32: All this is vanity, for by doing the good deed for the sake of the Blessed Creator alone, your words of rebuke will be accepted by the world even if you do not think this way, for the acceptance of rebuke does not depend upon your own thoughts.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:33: And after you have removed yourself from all this, the inclination will incite you and say to you: "Your service cannot be complete unless you distance yourself from these things entirely — for instance, that you should conceal your good deeds, and act the opposite of what was really in your heart: pray briefly, and when you wish to study some wisdom, do so in private, so that no one should know of it but the Blessed Creator. And show no good trait at all, but rather display laziness in the performance of the service, so that you not gain a reputation and lose your reward. And do not command what is good nor warn against what is evil, and do not make your wisdom known to any other man, and show no sign or mark of the fear of Heaven, such as tefillin, mezuzah, and tzitzit; rather, conduct yourself as they do and follow their ways, and mingle with them in eating and drinking, in merriment and much laughter." All this is among the schemes of the inclination to catch people in its net, and one who does this thinking it is for the sake of a commandment loses a thousand times a thousand more than his reward, and is like one who flees a small fire into a great one.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:34: Rather, the straight path is this: to pray at length with intention, to command what is good and warn against what is evil, and to do all good deeds both openly and in secret. And if people honor and praise him for this, the praise does him no harm, since he did not intend it at the time of the deed. Therefore, at the time you do a good deed, examine yourself as to from whom you hope for reward: if from God, it is complete; but if from others, it is not complete. And also examine whether, in this deed that you do before the world, you would have done the very same thing in private, in your innermost chambers, as you do it in public — and if this becomes clear to you, then your deed is complete.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:35: Everything we have related against the evil inclination is but a drop from the sea compared to what one is obligated to be careful of, for in every matter, in every deed, and in every trait, the inclination comes to corrupt and to ruin. And we have opened a door to make known the matter of the inclination to one who did not know its ways at the outset. And the wise man will understand, and hasten to remove it from within himself, "and the pure of hands shall grow stronger and stronger" (Job 17:9).
Orchot Tzadikim 1:36: Pride in the virtue of wisdom is praiseworthy, as it is said (Jeremiah 9:23), "but let him that glories glory in this, that he understands and knows Me." And he should add thanksgiving to the Blessed Creator, and also give thanks in prayer for his understanding, his intellect, and his good traits, saying: "I give thanks before You, that You have set my portion among those who sit in the House of Study, and not among those who sit idle on street corners," and likewise: "Happy are we, how good is our portion, and how pleasant is our lot." And of this it is said (2 Chronicles 17:6), "and his heart was lifted up in the ways of the Lord." For a person should be of noble spirit and lofty of heart in matters concerning the World to Come, so that he not be satisfied with whatever comes to hand, nor say "enough" with whatever he has managed to attain; rather, he should regard all his deeds as small in his own eyes, and let his soul aspire ever upward, and grieve within himself as though he falls short in the service of the Blessed Creator. And this pride does not harm humility but rather assists it, and causes him to rejoice in his good qualities, and to rejoice in the honor of his fellows and to be considerate of their honor.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:37: And pride shown against the wicked is very praiseworthy — to rebuke them and put them to shame, and not to submit to them; and he should command the good and warn against the evil to the best of his ability, even though this appears in the eyes of the world like domineering and pride, since his heart is for the sake of Heaven, this is praiseworthy. And he should not submit to the wicked, like Mordechai, who did not submit to Haman (Esther 3). And wherever there is a commandment to be done, he must do it, and not submit at all to the wicked by abandoning the good out of self-abasement before them. And this requires wisdom: when should he assert himself against them in a matter of a commandment? For sometimes it is not worthwhile for him to stand against them, since if he shows them a bold face for the sake of one commandment, he may cause them to lose a hundred commandments.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:38: Therefore the wise man must consider carefully, according to the time and the matter, and order his deeds accordingly; for there is a matter one must forgo for their sake, and there is a matter one must not forgo for their sake under any circumstances. And with his body and his substance he must stand against them, and not submit to them. And all this applies to a matter of commandment; but in a matter of business dealings, he should submit to them and act with them beyond the strict letter of the law in every matter — and this is a great commandment.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:39: And whoever has the trait of pride within him must strive to turn away from it, for it is very despicable, and its harm is great and constantly present, while its benefit is slight; therefore one must distance himself from it greatly, for pride brings a person to ruin and lowliness, as it is said (Proverbs 16:18), "Pride goes before a fall," and it is said (ibid. 29:23), "A man's pride shall bring him low." You already know what happened to Pharaoh when he said (Exodus 5:2), "Who is the Lord..."; and to Goliath the Philistine, who said (1 Samuel 17:10), "I have taunted the ranks of Israel"; and to Sennacherib, who said (Isaiah 36:20), "Who among all the gods of the lands has delivered their land from my hand, that the Lord should deliver Jerusalem from my hand?"; and to Nebuchadnezzar, who said (Daniel 3:15), "And who is the god that shall deliver you out of my hands?" — and to all who spoke like them; and their end was shame and disgrace. And whoever has this trait cannot be saved from sin and iniquity, as the wise man said (Proverbs 21:24), "Haughty, insolent, scoffer is his name, he acts in the fury of insolence."
Orchot Tzadikim 1:40: And since our words have reached this point in speaking of pride, hear the words of the wise. One wise man said: who is it from whom worry never departs? He who seeks to rise to a level that is above him. And they said: whoever holds himself to be knowledgeable, people hold him to be a fool. And they said: close beside pride are evil deeds; and whoever has evil deeds will be hated by his fellow creatures, and souls will turn away from him. And one wise man said: just as pleasantness of form is the light of the body, so pleasantness of character is the light of the soul.
